utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case Number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you follow the proceedings, and I take it since you answered, that you are following the proceedings in a language you that can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Julian Nicholls with Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Good morning to you both. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with David Cunningham, and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to the three of you. Any preliminaries before we proceed with the cross-examination? All right. Mr. Ackerman, the witness is once more in your hands. I don't need to ask you to repeat the solemn declaration. You will be You will be continuing your testimony under the same solemn declaration that you entered into yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. Ackerman. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's okay. We're used to the delays because of the translation. We were -- when we concluded yesterday we were talking about the -- let's see if I can remember exactly where we were. It was actually paragraph 1.114 of your report that we were discussing, and that had to do with Brdjanin touring combat areas, as you put it. I was wondering if you have ever heard of members of the British parliament visiting British combat areas, visiting commanders, getting briefings about what's going on militarily in conflicts that the British have been involved in.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me read this. All right, okay. Go ahead, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I take it you've also heard of or even seen on TV US senators and congressmen visiting zones of combat that the American forces are involved in?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I've -- I'm aware of that and seen it on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I take it you wouldn't take the position that just because they make these visits, it implies that they have some sort of control over those military structures, does it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I can be in a position to fully answer that, that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think you certainly know the chain of command of both the British and American military, and I think the Yugoslav military was similar. The civilian control was in the commander in chief, nowhere else, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe if I can break your statement down into its component parts. I am aware to some degree of the British chain of command. I'm not quite so au fait with the American military chain of command. The Yugoslav military was not exactly -- it was similar in some respects, but it was different in a lot of others, certainly to my military. Having looked at their -- many of their documents and some of their doctrinal material, it is notably different to the British Army. So I'm not sure that I would necessarily agree with you fully there. Civilian -- clearly civilian control, the commander in chief controls the army. He's usually head of the army. And in the case of the VRS, Radovan Karadzic was the commander in chief. But it's not quite as simple as that, as I articulate, I think, in the report. And also, it's articulated in many of the documentation -- much of the documentation. The military documentation I've reviewed. There was significant influence of civilian authorities at various levels, not just the commander in chief. So in trying to break down your question into its component parts, I think it's not as simple as you state in your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you basically telling us that it varies? It depends on who actually visits the combat zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For example, if it's your secretary for the defence or minister for the defence who is a civilian authority, or your prime minister, who is also a civilian, head of the executive, visits the combat zone --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would that tie up with what Mr. Ackerman asked you in the first place? The suggestion is visiting the combat zone doesn't mean at all that there is any measure of control or command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to answer the question, I think you're right. I believe that it depends who's visiting. In some respects it might not necessarily indicate a degree of control over the military. But in other cases, it might very well indicate some sort of influence or control over the military. And your example, Your Honour, that you quote, the minister of defence visiting British forces, for example, minister of defence is not the commander in chief of the British Army. But clearly, when the minister of defence visits the British Army and comes to get briefed, he is a significant player and a significant actor and has significant authority over the actions of the military. So I think the question is, it does actually depend on who's visiting. It can mean that, but it also might not mean that, to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's see if we can -- let's see if we can clarify that issue by looking at one of the military documents which I'm quite certain you've seen. I think maybe you even refer to it in your report. It's Exhibit P1569. What you should be looking at is an order, 5th corps command order dated 14 May 1992 signed by General Talic. And what I want to direct your attention to is paragraph 4. Paragraph 4 reads: "All requests for assistance, cooperation, and coordination of activities on the ground issued by civilian structures should be forwarded to the corps command which shall resolve them in cooperation with the municipal authorities or pass them on to the 2nd military district command." Correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And doesn't this indicate that civilian structures may make requests only, not issue orders, that those requests must go to the corps command, or maybe even to the 2nd military district command? That even the local units had no authority to grant such requests. Right?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: This instruction does state as it states, that requests for assistance from -- or cooperation and coordination issued by civilian structures should go to the corps command, and that may need to be forwarded to the 2nd military district command. But there are many other documents, are other documents which indicate, for example, that some of the municipalities where orders were being issued at Crisis Staff decisions. This instruction from Talic, I would imagine, is attempting to formulate the relationship between the civilian structures and his corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've raised an interesting question to some extent by your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. answer, and it's one that has, I suppose, great significance. There is nothing in the world that would prevent me from ordering you to do something. I could sit here right now and order you to, you know, stand on your head in front of the Court. Whether or not I have the power to do that's a completely matter, and that would depend on whether you believe that you are compelled to follow that order. And so just because a Crisis Staff issues some kind of an order to the military doesn't mean they have the power to do so, does it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I can answer that. My report is not about the nuanced or details about legal authorities of Crisis Staffs or political institutions. So I'm not sure I can answer that from my competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's a common sense question. You mean, you have common sense. It's a common sense question. Just because someone orders someone to do something, doesn't mean they have the power to do that, does it? Just like I ordered you to stand on your head doesn't mean I have the power to make you stand on your head. The question is whether the person to whom the order is directed believes that it's binding, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I see point he's trying to make, but I really don't see the value of this type of hypothetical question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is some value to it. I will allow it. What I would add, to make it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, what I could add to round it up is perhaps that -- I've had some experience in diplomacy, too. The recipient of the "order" might prefer to call it a "request." We could be speaking of the same thing. From one point of view, it's an order, from the other point of view it's classified as a request, in order not to enter a confrontation, or even at least to give it some kind of recognition, and not brush it aside as an unlawful or -- an unlawful order. I don't know. I mean, I'm just suggesting this to the witness, perhaps the witness, being a military analyst, knows better than all of us put together here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would hypothetically agree, yes, if someone issues an order, then you would assume that there was some -- someone would, as you say -- you know, if they were to execute that order, that they would have some authority over it. In terms of this document, I believe what Talic is doing is saying here we have a situation where we need to ensure a coordinated approach. I have my competencies. We must ensure that requests, whether coming from civilian authorities, are dealt with in the appropriate chain. And I need to be aware of it. And if there are difficulties, we might send up to the 2nd military district. The request could include orders, decisions, simple requests for assistance. I'm not sure. But I think this instruction is an instruction to improve the command and control within the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, that's an answer giving it the best interpretation you can give in favour of the Prosecution's position, isn't it, what you told us when you started yesterday was not your task?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's not fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls. He's asking him whether this is more in line -- no, it's a perfectly legitimate question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just think it's for Your Honours to decide how the answers fall, not the witness. The witness is here to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman is suggesting that since the witness is giving an interpretation to this paragraph number 4 from this document, it's being suggested, it's being put to him that out of all the interpretations possible, he's chosen the one which fits most or best your case rather than the Defence. And I will allow it. Of course I will allow it. He is perfectly capable of handling this kind of -- if he was another kind of witness, maybe he would require some kind of assistance from the Trial Chamber. But not the present witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe I'm trying to give the best interpretation for the Prosecution at all. I'm looking at the document from my military experience. And I see a document from General Talic which is dealing with issues of command and control of his corps. He clearly wants to ensure that requests for cooperation and assistance from civilian authorities are dealt with in an appropriate manner. And that's what I believe the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us you had seen some instances where local units seemed to be responding to Crisis Staff orders or requests. Maybe this is an effort by General Talic to stop that. Make it clear that they ought not be doing that, that those requests should be forwarded up to higher authority. Is that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not necessarily sure it's an attempt to stop those requests or orders or decisions. I think it's an issue about General Talic as a corps commander improving the command and control within his corps and wanting to know what requests are coming into the units. It doesn't say in paragraph 4, "all requests for assistance and cooperation are to be stopped." I think this is an issue about command and control of the corps. It's being ensuring that he's made aware and that the competencies are dealt with in the appropriate way, and he's trying to improve or to, as he states, improve command and control of units within the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, maybe you misunderstood my question. I wasn't suggesting it was an order that requests should stop. I'm suggesting that it might have been an effort on General Talic's part to remind the local units that they are not to respond to those requests; they're to forward them on up the chain.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question earlier on, you did say, this is an effort of General Talic to stop that. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I meant to stop those units from responding to those requests. To instruct them that they should be forwarded up the chain, not dealt with locally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a straight answer. Yes or no. Reading that paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Reading that paragraph again, and also reading perhaps between the lines, that paragraph and the rest of the document, could you agree with what is being suggested to you by Mr. Ackerman? And you can just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think it's a request to stop responding to these requests. It's to forward these requests to the corps so it can be dealt with in the appropriate manner. And so that the corps is informed. I believe that's what paragraph 4 is stating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to something else, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm doing. Let's look at a new document, P227, please. And this is a long document. I'm going to refer you to page 26 of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which page, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 26, Your Honour. It's item 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is about a week later. I think the prior document was 14 May. This one is 22 May. It's conclusions from a meeting of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. The paragraph I want to direct your attention to is paragraph 4 which reads: "In view of the present poor coordination between the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the newly established army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, mandatory attendance of General Talic or a person designated by him is requested - note the word`requested' - at the meetings of the Crisis Staff." Now, this seems to indicate that neither General Talic nor any person from the 5th/1st Corps had been attending Crisis Staff meetings, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether they had been attending Crisis Staffs prior to this date. That reference doesn't say that. The reference says there has been poor coordination. That may well indicate that there was no Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. attendance or limited attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, does it make sense that they would be requesting General Talic or a person designated by him to attend meetings of the Crisis Staff if they had already been attending them? I mean, obviously that implies that they hadn't been and they would like them to, doesn't it? Why else write that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, clearly they want a representative from the corps to attend -- or they're requesting an attendance from the corps. Whether that -- prior to that there had been sporadic attendance or limited attendance or no attendance, I can't say. But, yes, you're right. I mean, clearly they want a corps member to attend the ARK Crisis Staff based on this section. And in fact, I think I reference this in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 1.116, on page 51, is exactly where you referenced it in your report. Let's go now to another document, P1461. This is a -- and please understand as I told you yesterday that you are always free to read the entire document if you feel you need to.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no intention of restricting you to parts of it, but I will direct your attention to parts of it. This is a document from the command of the 1st Krajina Corps sent to the Main Staff of the VRS. It's a regular combat report. And the date is 23 September 1992. I'm interested in paragraph 3. The last sentence of that paragraph, the paragraph is about the situation in the territory in the zone of responsibility. "There are increasingly frequent raids by uncontrolled armed groups on Muslim and Croatian villages (e.g. Cela village near Prijedor, and Majdan village near Mrkonjic Grad) for the purpose of plunder and liquidation of people." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So by 23 September 1992, apparently there were Muslim and Croatian villages near Prijedor and Mrkonjic Grad that still had their populations and were being raided by these uncontrolled armed groups; I assume paramilitaries of some kind. True?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would seem to indicate that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's go now to paragraph 1.128 of your report. And you talk about the 16th Assembly meeting again of 12 May and the words of Mr. Brdjanin. And what you report there what he said: "How can anyone still believe it is right that we have a Muslim teaching political classes in the Banja Luka Corps?" Now, by this time, 12 May 1992, war has broken out between Serb forces and Muslim/Croat forces, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combat activity had occurred in April and in early May in some municipalities in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Between Serb forces and Muslim/Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some areas between forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Wouldn't you say from a military standpoint that this is a wholly sensible position, a military security standpoint, that you wouldn't have someone whose loyalties might be to those who you are fighting against teaching political classes to your own corps? Isn't that a sensible security thing?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you simply base it on his ethnicity as opposed to going further in terms of checking his loyalty or whether he himself potentially wanted to remain within the Serbian army, then I'm not necessarily sure I'd agree with you. It's not always the case that just because -- they should all be removed, all the non-Serbs should be removed necessarily because of their ethnicity which seems to be the case that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're not talking about all the non-Serbs. We're talking about one person teaching political classes in the Banja Luka Corps who is a Muslim. I'm not talking about all non-Serbs now. I'm talking about one person. We know who that is, too. It's Colonel Hasotic, I think.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was Colonel Hasotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe I can ask the question in a different way. I think it would be highly unlikely that, especially during the times when there were open hostilities going on, that there was a member of the IRA teaching political classes in the British Army or a Syrian in --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to object to this whole line. I mean, I think it's just a silly analogy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection sustained, Mr. Nicholls. I think the witness had understood your previous question, Mr. Ackerman, and he doesn't need to be referred to any particular example, especially considering that he was part of the British Army in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this, then: Are you aware that at least one Muslim officer in the JNA was passing sensitive information while serving in the JNA to Muslim authorities in Sarajevo? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you be more specific in terms of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, it's being suggested to you that perhaps Mr. Hasotic himself was playing the double game.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to go into private session, and then I'll be more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 1.130, we're now several days later. And the ARK Crisis Staff expresses its concern with regard to a large number of Muslim and Croat officers still serving in units in the Banja Luka area. Again, expressing their concern from a security standpoint. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wonder if it's possible for me to look at that document again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, P1582 I believe is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I can tell Mr. Brown, that's footnote 221 in your report, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The document you see is a 9 June 1992 1st Krajina Corps document. Colonel Milutin Vukelic reporting on the meeting of the ARK Crisis Staff from the day before. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the second paragraph, the second sentence: "An ultimatum was issued requesting - and I note the word`request' again - removing these persons from vital command posts by 15 June 1992 or they will take over the control of the OS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, we need to push the paper a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So not only was the Crisis Staff expressing its concern, security concern apparently, regarding the non-Serb officers serving, but even -- one way to read this is that it was the Crisis Staff that threatened to take over control of the army. Right?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the basis of this document. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What do you think the likelihood was that a few guys sitting on that Crisis Staff could take over the army? Zero?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can competently answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the rest of the document, it says this: "We - and I don't know exactly who `we' is, but it's Colonel Vukelic and whoever he considers `we' - consider their demand to be justified. But it is impossible to find adequate professional replacements among the reserve staff and active officers of BH origin are not arriving from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Such action would significantly weaken the above-named units from which it has been requested that the staff be purged. We are aware of a certain degree of danger, and we are excluding such persons from the more important decision-making processes. Our recommendation is to accelerate the process of sending active soldiers of BH origin over from FR Yugoslavia. The 1st Krajina Corps command should make the decision as to which staff members from the ranks of Muslims and Croats may still be temporarily kept at what posts." So what Vukelic is saying there, the Crisis Staff issued this ultimatum and a threat and everything else, and we're not going to do any of that. It doesn't make sense, so we're not going to honour that request.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's the case at all. And in fact, I believe this request was actioned and that officers of Muslim and Croat nationality were removed. And in fact, on the same day, there came down a request from General Mladic that officers of Muslim and Croat nationality should be sent on leave and their status should be reviewed in Belgrade. So I think also from the language of the corps report, that the general thrust is that the corps accept and agree that this is a policy that she should be implementing, but that there are some practical limitations that they may have in trying to replace these personnel because it would have some affect on the units that they're serving in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, just looking at the document, I agree with you, Vukelic is saying the demand is justified from a pure security standpoint. But all we can do now is -- you know, he says there's a degree of danger. All we can do right now is exclude them from important decision-making processes. What we might be able to do later is another matter. But we cannot comply with this request now. I mean, that's what it's saying, I think. I mean, if I'm reading it wrong, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the corps are sending this to the Main Staff and the Presidency of the SRBiH for a decision on what should happen. And what does happen is what the ARK Crisis Staff had asked, which was that -- actually requested in their ultimatum was that Muslim and Croats were to be removed from the corps. And Mladic's instruction which followed on the same day, later that same evening, was quite blunt in saying send Muslims and Croats -- nationality on leave and back to Belgrade where their status would be reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the 67 officers of Muslim or Croatian nationality -- or where did you get that back to Belgrade business that you just said?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can just bear with me for a second. I think -- I'd have to look again at the document, it may not mention Belgrade as a place. But I think footnote 223, the Main Staff instruction states that all superiors of Muslim and Croat nationality were to be sent on leave immediately and action was to be taken to refer them to the Army of the FRY where their status would be resolved. Again, it might be worth looking at that document to see if it does mention Belgrade. But in essence, they were to be sent on leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it important, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could just say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- I don't normally make this type of objection, but Mr. Ackerman does quite frequently. He said a couple of times "from a pure security standpoint from Vukelic," regarding this exhibit P1582 talking about removal from a pure security standpoint. Those words don't appear in the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm always grateful for the assistance of Mr. Nicholls, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, if you'll look what Vukelic says is we are aware of a certain degree of danger. I assume he's talking about security issues when he talks about being aware of danger. I don't think he believes they're going to blow things up, is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not make an argument. I mean, Mr. Nicholls made a suggestion. You noticed Mr. Ackerman that the Trial Chamber did not comment on it. I suppose it's not as important as Mr. Nicholls thinks it is. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the 67 officers of Muslim or Croatian nationality mentioned in this document?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know what happened to the 67 or who the 67 necessarily are. I do know, again, from listening to some of the testimony, for example, of -- one of the JNA colonels, he was -- they were removed. But Colonel Hasotic no longer appeared on documents -- well, in fact, Colonel Vukelic took his place. But as to the 67, I do not know. Having looked at the -- many of the 1st Krajina Corps military documents, predominantly corps-level material, some brigade-level references, I see -- I don't see many Croat and Muslim officers in positions of authority based on those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you do know that a significant number of former JNA officers of Muslim and Croat nationality wound up in the armies of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Forces and units of that nature?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe they did. Either Territorial Defence officers or JNA. It's not within the competency to know it all, but I generally do accept that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you also will accept that Muslims and Croats also continued to serve in the VRS throughout the entire conflict, won't you?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the ethnic breakdown of the VRS, and I don't know the ethnic breakdown of the 1st Krajina Corps. I am aware of a limited number, I believe, of Muslims and Croats, but a very, very small number that I've seen. But I cannot be accurate in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the suggestion is and what you are agreeing with is that the purge, if there was a purge, was not a complete, hundred per cent one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Take a look now -- I'm sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let the witness answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this document and the instruction from Mladic that followed was targeted clearly at officers of command and positions of authority. I cannot tell you what happened to those 67, but I don't know who the 67 are. I can tell you in the documents that I've reviewed from the 1st Krajina Corps, that I cannot remember seeing any Croats or Muslims in positions of authority in the corps at the corps level or in the brigade-level material that I've reviewed. I haven't looked lower. In terms of Muslims and Croats throughout the whole corps, I am -- I believe I would have to go back and refresh my memory, but I do believe that there were a small number of Muslims and Croats who served at low-rank soldiers. Maybe some were in mix marriages. Maybe some Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. responded. Maybe some wanted to stay in the VRS. I don't know. But I am aware of a limited number, but in terms of the overall numbers, it was very small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next document I want you to look at is P675, please. Now, this is another regular combat report of the 1st Krajina Corps command to the Main Staff. And the part I want to refer you to is page 2, and this is a section on state of security and morale again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Top, top, top paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 2, second paragraph on that page, beginning with the language: "Another unfavourable influence is the general tendency to rid the units of officers of Muslim and Croatian nationality because there are people among them who have from the first days wholeheartedly fulfilled all their assignments. Many among them do not have anywhere to go and cannot return to their ethnic communities. We propose that the purging of ranks be conducted openly, but based on the assessment of each unit. Officers who have opted to leave the ranks of the FRY army are ever more often asking when and how that will be done." And this is a report from General Talic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dated when, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is 11 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a question, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at 1.131 on page 56 of your report, you refer to that exact language that we just read, and then you put in parenthesis this, when you said they had no place to go. You say: "Presumably either because they may not have been welcome or because many of the ethnic communities referred to were damaged, besieged, or destroyed." Now, purely something that you -- a presumption that you put in your there yourself. That doesn't come from this report, does it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The issue with the VRS regarding these Muslim and Croat officers, I suggest to you, was a loyalty issue, a security issue, and not an ethnic issue. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think for some, there may well have been an issue of loyalty. Some of these Muslims -- well, potentially many of the non-Serb officers had served in the JNA for some time alongside officers within the -- who had been JNA officers in the VRS, and for some, maybe they felt, as this indicates, that, you know, they would fulfilled their tasks and there was no real reason why they should be removed. There would have been undoubtedly some element of security issue. So from the VRS's perspective, yes, there might well have been. Whether that was the driving factor for those outside the VRS, as I say in my report, I think to some degree you can't separate out what had happened within the VRS as to what was going on in other walks of life in the Krajina. Only a month or two beforehand, you'd had the issuance of the law on internal affairs which involved the division of the police and loyalty oaths and the like being disseminated out within the branches of the police which in essence separated and removed large numbers of police -- non-Serbs from the police in the Krajina. You also had issues relating to individuals being in positions of authority in civilian structures and managerial positions, either slightly later than this or around this period of time. So whether there may well have been issues from the VRS's perspective that it did cause some difficulties both in terms of replacing individuals from units that they might have felt were key or whether there was residual loyalty to persons who they had served with over a period of time during the JNA ranks, whether there were issues relating to security. I don't think you can exclusively take those out without also looking at the fact that this was as much about ensuring control over an important organ of power in the RS. You know, in the same way that that happened in the police and other situations. But I would agree that the -- for the VRS, it may well have included issues of loyalty and security. But I think the issue goes wider than just removing those people based exclusively on a security issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's take a look at what General Mladic thought about the position of the ARK Crisis Staff regarding the removal of all non-Serb officers and whether you still contend that it was implemented. Look at DB271, please. As you said, that report of Colonel Vukelic, it was sent up to the Main Staff. This is a document dated 16 July 1992 signed by General Mladic. He says this: "All officers of Muslim or Croatian nationality who are judged by the commands of corps and independent units to have proved themselves in combat action and who want to sign the oath and give a written statement that they accept citizenship of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they remain in active military service in the army of the Serbian Republic of BH". And then if you look at DB272, the document simply three days later signed by General Talic, responding to this document from General Mladic, General Talic then says: "All officers of Muslim or Croatian nationality who in the opinion of the brigade commands, independent units, and corps command, or headquarter support units have proved themselves in combat action who want to sign the solemn declaration and a written statement that they will take on the nationality of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina may remain in active military service in the army of the SRBH." Right?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I reference this document, I believe, in my report as well, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So both General Mladic, and then carrying out his directive General Talic, say that you don't have to be a Serb to serve in the army of the VRS. Muslims and Croats can serve in this army as long as we are willing to be citizens of SRBH and be loyal to SRBH. So it's not an ethnicity issue, it's a loyalty issue, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, clearly he does modify his position a month or so later in relation -- as the documents highlight. He does place conditions that they have to be -- have to prove themselves in combat, and the issue of loyalty oaths, and accepting SRBiH citizens, that they will be allowed to stay in the army. And I would argue that he may well have felt that removing so many key positions or some key positions may have had an effect on the VRS. The VRS were always short of officers, active military officers. And he may well have felt that the instruction that was passed out immediately needed to be amended and that these conditions were to be placed on Muslims and Croats in order for them to serve in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You just he modified his position later. Who are you talking about that modified their position?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic's order is different, the one on the 9th of June and this one in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the question I asked you was probably relatively simple. Based on these two documents, what these two generals are talking about is not an ethnicity issue but a loyalty issue. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this order allows for, under certain conditions, officers of Muslim and Croat ethnicity to remain in the VRS if they fulfill those conditions, which are loyalty, proven in combat, and are to take citizenship or nationality of the Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I take it you wouldn't suggest to this Chamber that the VRS was required to keep officers of Muslim and Croatian nationality in the army who were disloyal to the army. Certainly they're not required to keep those people, are they? No army in the world is required to keep disloyal officers. Don't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move forward in your report to paragraph 2.8. You say: "It should be noted that the mobilisation of the Bosnia-Herzegovina TO announced in early April by Alija Izetbegovic added significantly to the level of distrust. And in some areas, Serbs and the military were also Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the target of attack. This occurred in some locations where the non-Serb population had organised themselves or taken control. Serbs were moving out of some Krajina areas. There were reports of intimidation and theft." The first thing I want to ask you about that is: Isn't it the case that Izetbegovic ordered mobilisation of the BH TO before there was any order for mobilisation of TO units within the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just direct me to the section of my report again because you said 2.8, and I'm not sure that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 63.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Maybe there are two 2.8.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is. There is 2.8 and 2.80. Maybe I should have put it as 2.08. I do not know the full details of the Bosnian government's activities and decisions. That wasn't within the remit of the report. But I am aware that the Bosnian government announced a mobilisation of the TO in -- I think around the 5th or 6th of April 1992. As a result of activities that or in part activities that had gone on in Bijeljina municipality and some of the Drina area municipalities in late March and the first few days in April, the attacks in Bijeljina and Arkan arriving in Bijeljina and other areas. Also activity had happened in Sarajevo. So there was a series of events around late March and early April. And I believe that the Bosnian government in response to that, I think, potentially in part because they felt the JNA had not intervened in the likes of Bijeljina, to mobilise or to announce the mobilisation of the TO. So it was prior to, for example, the Serb mobilisation on the 15th and 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's look at another document now, P937. What you should be seeing is a regular combat report of 30 May 1992. I want to first direct your attention to the first paragraph of this report and the last sentence in that paragraph under number 1: "Last few days, Muslim and Croatian families are stopping at nothing to find ways of moving out of the areas affected by the war. Men fit for fighting are remaining in the area, however." And then if you go to paragraph 3, and that would be on the next page, near the bottom of that paragraph, I believe again: "The situation in Jajce continues to be unstable. The arrival of reinforcements from the direction of Bugojno has been observed as well as the strengthening of forces along the Donji can you have/Bugojno axis." Now, what's being talked about there are the opposing forces, the Muslim forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this last reference in Jajce and Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it was Muslim forces or Croat forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. But non-Serb. They're talking about the enemy basically.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then: "The emigration of the Serbian population from Bugojno is continuing." So the two parts I'm interested in there are in the first part we talked about families, Muslim and Croatian families are trying to find ways of getting out of war-affected areas. We go over to the next page, we find that the Serbian population is emigrating from war-affected areas. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this report, yes, the both of them do couch the movement as you state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I mean, that's a phenomenon of war, when hostilities are going on in an area, the civilian population tries to get away to keep from getting killed. I mean, that's not an unusual thing, is it, in any war?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not necessarily an unusual phenomenon in warfare that refugees -- that you find refugees or people moving out. I think there are other references that I quote in the report, both in terms of military documentation, that also move to, or reference forcible movement, expulsions, rather than just the refugees who happen to be trying to avoid conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I discuss that significantly in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you'll agree that people just generally don't find it comfortable to live in places where there's no food, no electricity, where there are -- there's fighting going on, they're likely to get killed. People tend to get away from things like that, don't they. I mean, that's another common sense kind of question, I think.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a hypothetical yes, it is. In terms of this report, all I can say is what I see from the military documents, is that yes, there was an element that would indicate in some of the documents that refugees were moving away from conflict areas or combat areas, but equally, there are references which talk about forcible movement, which talk about transferring people, exchanging people, which talk about the forcible migration and phrases like that in the report -- which are mentioned in the report. So to couch -- you've put one particular aspect here in one particular report which does make reference to, if you like, emigration, but I would suggest that you should balance that with the other reports which talk about forcible movement and others. So...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, go ahead. If you're not finished, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't believe I asked you anything about expulsions and forcible movement. I only asked you about these particular things in that document. And I want to refer back again to the beginning of our discussion yesterday when you explained your role to the Chamber as trying to be an unbiased reporter. Were you being an advocate just now when you decided to go beyond the question and point out that there were also documents dealing with forcible expulsions? Were you kind of advocating on behalf of the Prosecution at that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, that's an issue for the Chamber. I think it's a silly question. It's not a question about a fact in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer it, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He can answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you being biased, Mr. Brown? Do you think you can accept the suggestion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm here to try and give as an impartial analyst a contextual balance to them two I reviewed from the military's perspective and the limitations that were placed on me and the limitations I placed on myself in terms of this report. I've conceded this document talks about emigration. Yes, it does. I've conceded that this document talks about the movement of Serbs emigrating from non-Serb areas and that that is a feature -- can be a feature of war. But to be balanced and to put it into context, if you take that one document in isolation, that's what it says. But I equally see other documents that make reference to other issues talking about the movement of people. Some documents make reference to forcible movements, mass emigrations, forced transfers, deportations, including emigrations and refugees. So I'm trying to articulate that it's -- yes, this is an issue. People do want to move away from conflict areas, I'm sure, the hypothetical. When we're talking about this document, you have to balance that with the other documents I've also seen. So that's all I can say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So your answer is that Mr. Ackerman should not interpret this as a bias on your part; rather, he should take it, and the Trial Chamber should take it, that you are trying to put everything in its own perspective.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hope so, and I'm doing the best of my ability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've got your answer, Mr. Ackerman. You may proceed with the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And with regard to forced transfers and deportations, that's not just restricted to non-Serb persons. There were Serbs who were forcibly Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. transferred and deported too, weren't there, out of Central Bosnia, out of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not within the remit of my report to look at that. As a generality, I'm sure that on all sides, that type of activity went on. I can't tell you in detail about Central Bosnia and other areas because I don't work on that area. But as a generality, that seems to be a feature within the conflicts in the Balkans on all sides. My remit was to look within the Krajina and look in particular at the military documents predominantly, and I've done so. And where I've seen those types of references, I've included them in my report. But I concede your point, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume you will agree that even though your remit was the Krajina area, that what was going on throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, and even more widely in Croatia, Serbia, and other places, certainly impacted what was happening in the Krajina, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please look at the last page of that document. And we get an indication, at least on 30 May of 1992 what the total strength of the corps was at the time. It indicates that the total strength, officers, noncommissioned officers, and soldiers was 38.726, the effective strength.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any sense at all, any information at all that would tell the Chamber what the effective strength of the opposing Muslim and Croat officers in the zone of responsibility of the 5th Corps at that time was? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. The documents themselves make very -- surprisingly make very little comment about often -- the strength of the enemy that they would -- that they're facing. This comes at the 30th of May when there were significant actions in places like Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc. But I don't see figures given in the Serb documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you make any effort to look at other documents to see if you could find out what the effective strength of the opposing Muslim/Croat forces was during this period of time? Did you try to find out?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I looked through the Serb documents, the Bosnian Serb police documents, and I looked, for example, in some of the municipalities to see whether there was reference to figures from armed groups that the Serbs were -- when they were in action against. I know Prijedor to some degree, having looked at Prijedor Municipality in the Stakic case, I don't see much documentation. I saw some documentation in relation to Prijedor. There were some references there to rudimentary armed groups, rudimentary formations which were relatively ill-equipped, certainly in comparison to the 5th Corps and 1st Krajina Corps. But I haven't come across large documents or information that would give me an idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How about up in the corridor? Did you make any effort to find out what the opposition was like in the corridor, the Muslim and Croat forces up there where all the fighting was going on?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, again, many of the documents in the corridor --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sometimes no is really good enough, if it's good enough with you. We do have a lot of ground to cover. I don't want to cut off your answers, but if you could just say yes or no that could be helpful to us. Maybe even easier on you because sometimes your long answers give me a new question.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll take your advice, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was rapidly being strengthened during the summer of 1992? If you don't know, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I do know that the army of the ABiH was not formed until July, I believe early July. But as to its strength and its structures and the units it commanded, I'm not aware of that. It's not within the remit of that report or my competency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you one more question about that. Do you know that by August of 1992 the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had a strength of 128.000 troops, 128.000 men? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's look at -- staying on this subject basically, let's look at another document before we break, DB273, please. Now, it is a regular combat report again, 7 May of 1992. Paragraph 3 is what I'm interested in. Do you have it yet?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, this is the 7th of May --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 7 May 1992 regular combat report?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't see any -- yes, that is. That's the number.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Under 3: "The situation on the ground, the situation in the territory of Jajce, Donji Vakuf, Bugojno, and Gornji Vakuf municipalities remains critical. And those parts -- we're just about to show that you were correct earlier. The HOS Croatian defence forces and the Green Berets, units are conducting an intensive mobilisation. There is calm in Jajce municipality without any incidents, but there's a high degree of concern among the population. The Serbs are mostly moving out of these areas of the country. The Serbs in the Kljuc Municipality region want to assert their authority over the entire area and are demanding that the battalions 3/1 of the 30th partisan division carry out this task." What I'm interested there again is just the indication that Serbs are moving out of the area, but I thought in fairness you should look at the entire paragraph. And it does show that, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it shows, as it stated, that Serbs appear to be moving out. I'm assuming they're referencing the Jajce area there. But yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, we can take our break now, and then we'll start back with P909. If we could have it ready when we come back?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, permission granted, Mr. Ackerman. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours are being handed the new DB269B. You'll remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- yesterday pointing out that the B/C/S had nothing to do with the English. Now it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've also provided, and you'll be receiving I suppose, today, some additional exhibits that you see here on the table, along with an updated exhibit list, submission number 2. And it's just part of the ongoing process. The list will continue to grow, but that's as much as I have been able to get done so far. So, I'm just working away at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, the next document we wanted to look at is P909. This is a document of 19 May 1992. It's a regular combat report. And I just want to very briefly refer to an item on page 3, the second paragraph there. You'll recall that we've looked at a couple of documents before this talking about the Bugojno and Jajce area. This is another such document. This one says: "The authorities in Jajce are refusing to admit that the Serbian population is exposed to pressure, that houses are being broken into, that there is looting and the like. Adequate measures need to be taken should such provocations continue." From these documents and from other documents you might have seen, in your view, were these places, Bugojno and Jajce, being ethnically cleansed of their Serb inhabitants by the Croat/Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't think I'm in a position to answer that question. It wasn't within the remit of my report, and I don't feel I can adequately answer that without researching that further and dealing with other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That's fine. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Let's look, then, at another document. P375, please. You can also go to paragraph 2.17 on page 66 of your report where I think you refer to this document. What you say in your report is this: "From military documentation, it is evident that the military were not only aware of the details of the ARK deadlines and gathering information in preparation for operations, but were also conscious that the planned actions to seize weapons and disarm the population was adding to tension in the area and increasing the likelihood of interethnic conflict breaking out." Now, what you said there was that, if you leave out some intervening language, the military were conscious that the planned actions to seize weapons and disarm the population was adding to tension in the area and increasing the likelihood of interethnic conflict breaking out. Is that a fair assessment of what you're saying there?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's based on the reference that's in that section. I'm not sure -- is this the same document as I've quoted here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I hope it is. I think it is. But just give me a second and we'll know. If you look at paragraph 3, it reads: "Since the deadline for handing over illegally owned weapons has expired and the Banja Luka MUP organs are making appropriate preparations to take away the weapons, people fear possible interethnic conflicts." Now, it's my assumption that that is what you're referring to when you make the statement that the military were also conscious that the planned actions to seize weapons and disarm the population was adding to tension in the area and increasing the likelihood of interethnic conflict breaking out. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's -- I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where this report says, "people fear possible interconflict conflicts." It doesn't say which people. It doesn't say whether it's the Serbs that are fearing it or the Muslims that are fearing it or the Croats or everybody. Would you interpret that that means that all citizens were in fear of possible interethnic conflicts?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only go by what the document says, and it doesn't make any specific reference to which ethnicity. I know that there were other documents from the 5th Corps in early May and late April that talk about tensions rising. I believe one or two, and I'd have to go through my report, do make reference to particular ethnic groups. But this one does not indicate. I'm assuming that it could include all ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go now to paragraph 2.18 of your report on page 66. "It is also evident that after the various ARK and CSB decisions were issued and the 14 May 1992 deadline expired, it was not exclusively the police that were to be involved in the disarmament process, but that the army also had a role to play in the disarming of the non-Serb areas." That's what you tell us. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the first document that you say supports that is P195. So can we look at P195, please. And that's the document referenced in your footnote 272. That's a two-page document, and you might want to take time to look it over. What I'd like you to do is show the Chamber in that -- where in that document you find support for, one, the army having a role to play; and two, the disarmament being limited to non-Serb areas.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a reference in the document that manpower and materiel needed for the implementation of planned activities (this activity can only be implemented by authorised officials and the military police of the Banja Luka Corps)." So there's a reference there that certainly the police of the Banja Luka military corps have got some involvement in this -- in these making concrete plans. In reference to the non-Serb areas, this document itself doesn't highlight it as non-Serb areas. However, I can only state that in the documents I've seen, in the actions that happened in May and late May in relation to disarming, that those took place in and against non-Serb -- non-Serb areas. And from the documentation I've reviewed in the military collections, I don't see or I didn't see any military activity directed against Serbian villages or Serbian groups. But if you want to take that one line in exclusion and say, "does this document and this footnote reference specifically make a mention to non-Serb areas?", no, I concede that it doesn't. But I've seen other --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've cited other documents, and we can look at those. We can look at the one you cited in footnote 273, that is P706. This is a report on the work of the Sanski Most public security station for six months in 1992, January through June. Unfortunately, it's quite a long report. I don't know if you'll be able to find in there support for, one, the army having a role to play; and two, disarmament being limited to non-Serb areas.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I read the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it would be unfair if you couldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Take as much time as you require.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I -- I haven't read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe if I can myself refer you to page 7 of the report, the paragraph -- last paragraph in the first half of the page starting with the words "in the second quarter." Is that maybe what you were referring to or what made you refer to this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think there are a number of references. There are one or two prior to that, too, Your Honour. On page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 5 as well, last sentence of the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 3, I think there's a reference to military operations conducted by units of the JNA, the Serbian army, against Muslim formations. There's a reference on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would ask you to restrict it to the tasks that your paragraph 2.17, if I remember well, refers to and what you were referred to by Mr. Ackerman in his question; namely, the involvement or participation of the army in the disarming process and which part of these documents show that the disarming was restricted to the non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's a reference on page 4. This refers primarily to territory populated by Muslims, the villages in question were Polje, Hrastovi, and a number of others. And to a lesser extent some of the places due to the military operations in some of those areas and open clashes. There's a reference there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That doesn't say anything about -- I mean, you're talking in this paragraph about the ARK and CSB decisions regarding disarmament and the disarmament process, and you tell us that the army had a role to play in that. And what I'm asking you is: Find in here where it says that the army played a role in disarmament. And secondly, that it happened in non-Serb areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In actual fact, does this document speak of disarmament as such, to start with? Let's start from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's a reference on page 2, second quarter, a state of emergency was proclaimed on the territory of Sanski Most Municipality, and military operations were conducted by units of the JNA, Serbian army, against Muslim formations, so the work of the public security station was conducted under quite different wartime conditions which were reflected, in fact, the policeman recalled wanted to disarm people, search, mop up terrain, protect facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Policemen. I'm asking you about army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interject, but maybe to speed things up, on page 5, there's a reference to the confiscation of weapons from citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think Mr. Nicholls is referring to the paragraph beginning "much of the work..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Exactly. But it still doesn't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. say that this was done by the military, by the JNA. So the question remains: Forget the previous document, 195, and concentrate on this one, 706. Is there anywhere, any part in this document that could justify you concluding that the JNA participated in the disarming process and that the disarming was directed to the non-Serb population as against the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before I answer that question, Your Honour, can I just ask Mr. Ackerman which footnote reference you're referring to when -- I think you said footnote reference number 273 in relation to Sanski Most. Footnote reference 273 I have is a Sanski Most Crisis Staff decision. It is not the CSB decision. Now, that is one issue slightly to clear up. Maybe I could look at footnote 273, which is the Sanski Most Crisis Staff decision, rather than this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you cite 01106424, and I think if you look, that is page 4 of this document. You're citing us to page 4 and 5 of this document in your footnote 273. Now, you said it was a Sanski Most Crisis Staff decision, but that was clearly in error; or your citation to those pages is clearly in error. One or the other.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there is an error in the footnote because -- which I need to clear up, I think. The Sanski Most Crisis Staff decision ERN 00471824 is different. This is the B/C/S ERN for the police document, an 00493711. I've clearly mistaken the translation and put down the translation for the CSB document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the date doesn't coincide either, huh?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So maybe we are -- I don't know. But definitely we don't have -- definitely 01106424 is the document that you're being shown now. That's Exhibit P706. That's where we have those ERN numbers. But then this is not a Sanski Most Crisis Staff decision, definitely not. And the document itself is certainly not dated 22nd of May 1992. Because what we have here is a Banja Luka security service centre report, six-monthly report if I take it well -- if I read it well, and it is dated 20th of July of 1992. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document, I have found it looking -- searching by the B/C/S ERN number. The document is P639. 23 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I do not have this, usher, so I suggest you put it on the ELMO and let us have a bird's-eye view of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's just a one-page document, Your Honour, so I think it's going to be easy to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that's the document you're referring to in the footnote, is it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you're probably referring to paragraph 3 of it.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that Territorial Defence and members of the 6th Krajina Brigade, which was a VRS or 1st Krajina Corps, also a JNA unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to jump in, Your Honour. What I have is the Sanski Most Crisis Staff decision dated 22nd of May of this ERN, 00471824 is P637. Again, 22nd of May. That's the number that matches the Exhibit P637.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And can I see the top of this document, have it on the ELMO. This is a Crisis Staff of Sanski Most decision taken on the 22nd of May -- 22nd. The document is dated 23rd of May. But the decision that it refers to is the one taken the day before. That's on the 22nd of May of 1992. And supposedly, it's a decision taken by the same Crisis Staff. So let's see 637 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, 00471824, which is the document he refers to in his footnote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- I have here on my screen now in the B/C/S version. It is -- that document that is designated something slash 24 slash 92, K something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the previous one, the one we saw before. This one that we have on the ELMO now which I'm seeing on my monitor, the document itself is dated 22nd May. It has a reference number, Crisis Staff 23/92, and the decision supposedly was taken the day before; that is, the 21st of May. So again, the two -- while the date on the previous document would coincide what we have here, it seems that this doesn't. I don't know what we are talking about. I suppose we should ask the witness. Have a look at 637 and 639, the two documents -- last two documents that you have been provided with, check the ERN number. Forget about the English translation ERN number because definitely that doesn't coincide. And tell us which one of the two you are referring to, if at all. Because you may have been referring to the -- something else for all I know. I can't see any of them because we don't have these two documents available. So I can't help.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe what I did, I was referencing Document Number -- ERN 00471824 to 1827, which is dated the 22nd of May which is the conclusion from the Serbian Municipality of Sanski Most Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of the 21st.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the 21st. Now, clearly the other document, 23rd of May referencing the 22nd of May, they're clearly linked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are talking about the same issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You only mention one here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do only mention one, and I think what I did was clearly put in the wrong translation ERN on the footnote. But I believe I'm referencing in this particular instance the document dated the 21st for the meeting that was held on 21 [sic]. But obviously those two documents are linked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to maybe shorten matters up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at P637 paragraph 4, as far as disarming paramilitary formations in Sanski Most is concerned, Colonel Basara and Colonel Ancic are charged with putting this into practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move forward, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's see if we can get the right document if we look at P924. This is, I believe, the document you cite in footnote 274. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you find the section you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's at the end of paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it "because of the situation in Kljuc"? Is that the one you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "Because of the situation in Kljuc, the 3rd Battalion of the 1st infantry brigade was made fully combat ready as ordered. If the Muslims do not surrender their weapons by 27 May 1992 at 1200 hours, the battalion will carry out a mopping up operation. To this battalion, BG2, has been attached and has been under our command since last night." Do you see any relation there between what's stated in that paragraph and the ARK or CSB decisions, deadlines? Isn't this purely a military operation here?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do see a relationship between the ARK decision on deadlines, as I've articulated in the report. I believe that you can document a flow between the issue of -- the number of decisions that were taken at the ARK region in relation to deadlines, the extension of deadlines, and action on the ground that subsequently followed in a number of municipalities. I articulated that, I believe, in my direct. I articulated that, I believe, in the Stakic case. And in this report from a brigade of the 30th Division, which was subsequently involved in operations in Kljuc, it makes mention of surrendering weapons. And I would argue that that alone with the other materials in other municipalities would indicate the decisions taken at the ARK region had an effect on the ground, and that military operations and also police operations because I believe a number of CSB reports talk about disarming operations in those municipalities, too, that those decisions were -- had an affect and resulted in military operations against in this case Muslim areas in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the document itself doesn't make that connection. That's a connection you make. That's a conclusion you draw, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, clearly the document itself does not say an ARK decision, doesn't mention an ARK decision. But if you take that document in isolation -- or if you take that document and place it with the other documents, I would argue that you can draw a conclusion that the ARK Crisis Staff decisions impacted and resulted in some municipalities on operations to disarm groups in those municipalities. And in this case, in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at one more document. And this is another big document, but I think we can work our way to where we need to be. It's DB282.
