In footnote 275 of your report, you refer to this as a 5th Corps/1st Krajina Corps notebook. I can't find where it says that on this document anywhere, that it's a 1st corps/5th Corps notebook. Is that just a conclusion you drew from its contents?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the original document. It's a notebook. It does come from the archive of the 1st Krajina Corps, and it is entitled "daily notes on the situation in the battlefield in the zone of responsibility."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I accept that. That's fine. I think the part you're referring to is on page 65 of the document where it says: "At 2200 hours, security organ BOGD..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "In Lisnja village, Prnjavor, the deadline for surrendering weapons was set for 1800 hours. They have done this, handing over about 47 rifles, mostly AP and PAP, and about 90 hunting rifles. When a group of about a hundred members of Prnjavor TO detachment, a group of extremists took these weapons and took to the woods. An exchange of fire ensued and the fighting is still underway. The road is blocked between Laktasi Prnjavor." Do you agree that's the entry you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, one could draw I suppose several different conclusions from this. One could conclude that by 1800 hours, people from Prnjavor, including Serbs, handed over their rifles in pursuance of the deadline. And then presumably a group of extremists, presumably non-Serb extremists, took the weapons, headed off into the woods, and there's a firefight going on. Certainly one conclusion you could draw from that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd agree that there are a number of conclusions. It's notes in a notebook. It's not a detailed report about the incident. It is some ambiguity there, and there could be a number of interpretations. I used this reference not necessarily for that, but to highlight that deadlines as an issue were being set, and that this also happened in the case of Lisnja village or Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's just assume for a moment that there is an effort being made to avoid fighting. If there's an effort being made to avoid fighting where ethnic tensions are increasing, like we have discussed earlier today, isn't trying to disarm people a possible way to avoid armed conflict? Isn't that something you kind of think of might keep armed conflict from breaking out? When a lot of people who are in conflict with each other all have guns, the likelihood of conflict is pretty high. Doesn't that make sense?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a hypothetical, that would make sense, to attempt to disarm. But if I can bring you back to what I view from the documents that I've seen and bring it back to my report, what I see were deadlines being imposed to disarm, deadlines being -- once those deadlines have expired, action on the ground taken by military and police units in certain municipalities to disarm groups or to conduct mopping up operations. And I didn't see that occurring in non -- in Serb areas. From the documents I've seen and the references to deadlines and the actions that followed, I see those actions occurring in non-Serb areas within the municipalities that I have been able to look at and that the documents -- the Serb VRS documents would indicate that. What I don't see here is a balanced attempt to disarm all groups in all areas either forcibly or through negotiation in order to diffuse the situation as you highlight in your hypothetical. What I see is deadlines being imposed very quickly in terms of the deadline, military action resulting from those. No long protracted period particularly. And I don't see it -- I don't see those actions occurring in Serb areas that I have been able to look at, able to see from the documents that I've seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think the one we're just looking at is illustrative of what you're just talking about. If you just look at what's there, not knowing any more, it appears that a deadline was set, that it was complied with, that weapons were actually surrendered, and that the conflict broke out when a bunch of non-Serb extremists then stole the weapons and started a firefight. That's what it looks like there, doesn't it? So, it looks like there was a successful effort to avoid it until these extremists stole the weapons and started shooting.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I say, I can't tell you from -- from just this notebook, what exactly occurred. It is an ambiguous entry. You portray a particular picture that you could argue from this. There are others, no doubt, that you could argue. I do know that there is a document and I believe from the 1st Krajina Corps daily combat report which makes mention of the operation in Lisnja and makes a mention that the population was expelled as a result of this. I think there's a reference to this in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we just look at the last part of that, I'm not sure that's ambiguous. "A group of extremists took the weapons and took to the woods. An exchange of fire ensued and the fighting is still underway." Now, it doesn't say they are Muslim extremists or Croat extremists. I guess one could conclude that it was Serb extremists and that there are Serbs fighting each other. But I think it more likely that it's non-Serb extremists who stole the weapons and that an exchange of fire followed. Don't you?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if it is -- I would imagine more likely that it would be non-Serbs, and they would couch often those armed groups as extremists, and that may well have been the case. Clearly it doesn't tell you how many weapons were stolen, clearly it doesn't tell you what happened during that exchange of fire. Clearly it doesn't tell you a lot of things. But that is one of the interpretations you could put on this slightly ambiguous and bulletised reference from a notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But it does say 137 rifles were turned in, 90 hunting rifles and 47 mostly automatic rifles. And then it says that a group of extremists took these weapons, and I assume "these" means the 137 that were turned in.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would seem to indicate that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It would, wouldn't it. All right, there's one more document in this line that we must look at quickly. It's DB283.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is another very long document. I think it's 82 pages long or something. I've just extracted three pages from it, because the witness gave a date and so I simply found the date and I think found the part that he's referring to and I'll ask him if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's on page -- I think you have the page 24 there, and there's one reference to Kotor Varos which your footnote refers to. And it simply says: "Kotor Varos, the village of Vrbanjci, they have not surrendered weapons." I assume that's what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that is probably is the reference. Again, I would -- it is a long document, I'd have to go through it, but I think that is the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is not so long if you consider the date that you refer to in your footnote, I don't think. You talk about the notebook entry for 15 June. And I tell you this is the only entry for 15 June that has anything to do with Kotor Varos or surrender of weapons. And I've got the full document here if you want to look at it.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. No, I'd rather not look through another 80 pages of document if I could avoid it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. So you accept that that's the reference that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to move now to paragraph 2.24. In that paragraph, you tell us about a little over halfway down: "in Sanski Most municipality, for example, the SDS appeared to have been notably influential. And according to their own documentation, at least, the Crisis Staff were in a position to instruct the TO units in a number of areas." The example you cite us to is Exhibit P621. And let's take a look at that, please. Do you have it now?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first thing you told us in your report dealt with the influence of the SDS. This document, however, is not an SDS party document but a Crisis Staff document from the Serbian democratic party -- yeah, it is, too. Serbian democratic party of Sanski Most Municipal board. Okay. You say that based upon this document, the Crisis Staff were in a position to instruct the TO units in a number of areas. Does this document deal with a number of areas?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, it may not be a number of areas, but it does make mention that the TO are to be placed at the disposal of the commander of the Serbian Territorial Defence and engaged as a special unit of the Serbian TO. I'll draw your attention also to the documents that we have just been discussing in relation to the Crisis Staff meetings in May whereby the Territorial Defence and 6th Krajina Brigade are being instructed to operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the language, exactly the language. "The Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Sanski Most here adopts the conclusion that the Serbian Defence Forces are to be placed at the disposal of the commander of the Serbian Territorial Defence and engaged as a special unit of the Serbian Territorial Defence." Now, that's what it says. Right?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any evidence whatsoever that the Serbian Defence Forces were actually placed at the disposal of the commander of the Serbian Territorial Defence in Sanski Most or ever engaged as a special unit of the Serbian Territorial Defence of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember if I have evidence. I'm not sure. I'm trying to think. I don't think I've referenced that in my report. I can't say one or the other, to be truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you tell us is they were in a position to instruct. And I suspect that's true. Almost anybody was in a position to instruct. The question is not whether they were instructing or not, but whether those instructions were being carried out, isn't it? It's the thing we talked about earlier, about my ordering you to stand on your head.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would argue that other documentation, certainly other references that I've put in this report would clearly indicate a significant influence, certainly in the period of time before the, if you like, the full and foremost establishment of the VRS, the significant influence of Crisis Staffs and the SDS on activities in municipalities that they wanted to control. The VRS themselves make a lot of references to that. In fact, I'm quite happy to drag out some of those references from the combat analysis readiness report of 1993 which talks significantly about, well not significantly, but makes a number of references when it's looking back to 1992 about the influence of the SDS and Crisis Staffs and bodies during that initial period to take control of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the question I'm really trying to, and I think you've answered it, you really don't have any evidence to indicate that this particular conclusion in paragraph 6 of these conclusions was ever implemented, that the Serbian Defence Forces actually were placed under the command of the Serbian Territorial Defence and is engaged as a special unit, do you?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, I can only go -- I do not remember -- I can't remember all the documents I've seen, so I can't say one way or the other whether I've seen evidence or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the answer as you sit here right now, you know of none. Isn't that a fair answer?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I sit here now, I cannot remember seeing any that would indicate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I invite you after you leave here today if you can find any evidence of that, please give it to Mr. Nicholls, and I will not object to it being admitted in evidence in this case. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's fair, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go now to another part of your report. Paragraph 2.58 on page 82. In that document, you refer to an exhibit, P400. It's actually in 2.59, I think. This is a document of 28 July 1992 written by Colonel Zdravko Tolimir, who was head of the department for intelligence and security affairs of the BH army Main Staff. Correct? Serbian Republic of BH Army Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what he is apparently seeking to do here is provide a report on the paramilitary formations operating in the territory of the Serbian Republic of BH. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a report, as it's entitled, on paramilitary formations on the territory of the SRBiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have quoted in your report a number of the findings that he made in there, that they are individuals of low moral quality. I'm not going to take the time to read everything you wrote there. But basically, he hasn't got any good things to say about any of these paramilitary groups, does he?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he clearly lists their characteristics, and some of them are quite blunt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, this report came out -- let's go back and just make sure we remember this date. This report came out on 28 July 1992. So keeping that date in mind, I'd now like you to look at another document. Keep that document with you. Look at another document, DB284, please. This is an order issued by General Talic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, this is P2500 as well, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's an order issued by General Talic two days later, on July 30th, is it not?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, in that order, General Talic is ordering disarmament of paramilitary formations. Right? Let's just go through it, starting in the first paragraph. In the first paragraph, he refers to some of the things that are contained in that report. For instance, he refers to looting as their principal motive. The second paragraph, he says: "A large number of paramilitary formations have declared themselves special-purpose units choosing tasks on which they spend one or two days, and then willfully withdrawing from the front which corrodes the morale of units that have been on the front line since the beginning of the war." The next paragraph, last sentence: "These illegal formations have also operated under the symbols of opposition parties, declaring themselves Chetniks or guard units with the intention of avoiding the front and organised armed combat under the command of SRBH Army." Down at the bottom of that page: "I hereby order, offer all paramilitary formations and their leaders if they do honestly intend to serve the rightful struggle for survival of the Serbian people, an opportunity to join regular SRBH Army units and assign them in accordance with their military occupational specialties and military skills." Number two: "Do not include in units individuals and groups which have been involved in crimes and looting or have committed other criminal acts, disarm and arrest them and bring criminal charges against them in SRBH Army courts, regardless of their citizenship. In cooperation with SRBH MUP, disarm and arrest paramilitary formations, groups, and individuals belonging to them who refuse to come under the unified command of the SRBH Army and bring criminal charges against them corresponding to the criminal acts they have committed." Number five: "I forbid the existence of any paramilitary units, groups, or individuals in the territory of the SRBH. From now on, bring criminal charges against those commanders, competent military territorial organs and government organs which enable to paramilitary organising and avoidance of recruitment and conscription in accordance with the law on the army of the SRBH." And in six: "By 15 August 1992 at the latest, disarm all paramilitary formations and submit a detailed report on this." So General Talic is responding to that report, and basically ordering disarmament of the criminal formations and inclusion of other formations into the army or their arrest or disarmament. I think that's a fair appraisal, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in generality, he outlines the issues of paramilitaries. He also makes mention about the fact that many of them are hiding behind legal forms of government and the likes. And he orders that they should be given the right to join the army and come under the command of the corps. He does in paragraph 2, as you rightly say, says don't include units who have been involved in crimes and disarm and arrest those ones. And in an attempt to bring these paramilitary groups into the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, keep that date in mind, 30 July. Look at your paragraph 2.65 on page 84.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is evident that despite General-Major Talic's own order, that individuals and groups that had been involved in crimes were not to be included in the corps. Some of the paramilitary units indicated in the Main Staff report were integrated into the corps structure. A good example of this was Veljko Milankovic and his group from Prnjavor." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I guess your purpose in that is to show that even though General Talic ordered on July 30th that paramilitaries that had been responsible for committing crimes should not be incorporated into the corps, that in spite of that order and in defiance of that order, Veljko Milankovic and his group were incorporated and integrated into the corps. That's what you're trying to suggest, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm saying that in this case, Veljko Milankovic, who was a known criminal, and there is CSB documentation that I refer to highlighting that, he also caused difficulties and problems within the military, but that he was integrated into the -- into General Talic's corps, and there is other information and documentation that he was given a rank and ammunition. And his group was given specific tasks, and in his case, I believe, he went off to the Knin in Croatia under an order and instruction by General Talic and to conduct an operation where he was wounded and subsequently died of his wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. 30 July, General Talic enters this order. You tell us that General Talic himself violated that order by integrating Veljko Milankovic into the corps structure. Look at your own report, 2.67: "On 5 June, 1992, Milankovic was given a rank, and his paramilitary group formally integrated into the 1st Krajina Corps structure on the order given by General-Major Talic." That's almost two months before this order, which you say he violated by bringing Milankovic into the 1st Krajina Corps structure.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying he violated in that respect, but he's including a character who from previous documentation had been involved in crimes. And I believe I'd have to go back to the CSB report on Milankovic, but there was reference to him being involved in looting --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Wait a minute. I'm sorry. I don't mean to -- we have to be clear. You just said to me I'm not saying he violated in that respect. Look at 2.65. "It is evident that despite General-Major Talic's own order that individuals and groups - that's referring to the July 30th order - that individuals and groups that had been involved in crimes were not to be included in the corps." Some of the very paramilitary units indicated in the Main Staff report were integrated into the corps structure. A good example was Veljko Milankovic. And the only time he was actually integrated into the corps structure was on 5 June, which you refer to in 2.67. So the connection doesn't exist, does it, that you're suggesting in 2.65?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're weaving and picking over some of the words. My point is that Veljko Milankovic was a known criminal from 1991, and a known paramilitary as well. General Talic's order on the 30th of July talked about not taking those who had been involved in crimes within the corps. And Veljko Milankovic was in the corps, and it would strike me that General Talic, who clearly knew Milankovic because we have an instruction in early 1992 where he is dispatched to Western Slavonia under the authority of General Talic when he was chief of staff of the corps, that here you have an acceptance that this man will play a part in the corps and be sent off on operations as dictated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's move to a different subject. Paragraph 2.76. Prior to that paragraph, you had talked about incidents in various areas. You're talking in paragraph 2.75, incidents against Serb forces, and you describe some of them in that paragraph. And then in 2.76, you say this: "Although some of these incidents caused the deaths of Serb soldiers and policemen and were carried out by armed Muslim and/or Croat groups who had some responsibility in raising the tension in these areas, it would be easy at face value to take their specific incidents and argue that they alone were the reason for every municipality attack." Are you suggesting here, and it's fine if you are, I just want to make it clear, that the attacks on Serb soldiers and Serb policemen and the killing of Serb soldiers and Serb policemen by armed Muslim or Croat groups were not sufficiently serious to justify the actions taken in response by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: In attempting to answer that, what I'm seeing here is accepting that there were a number of occasions where Serb soldiers and Serb policemen were killed, clearly by armed groups, non-Serb armed groups. But that that type of action didn't occur in every municipality that I've seen and that the response after or around those actions appeared to be a forceful, robust, and significant. And I would seem to -- it would seem to me that they were disproportionate to the individual incident that I have seen, such as in Prijedor, for example, they were disproportionate to those specific instances that I have seen. I have not argued in my report that -- and gone into the issues of disproportionality. That is a legal issue that I feel I am not competent necessarily to deal with. But from my perspective, from the documents I've seen, and from my own military experience, the relatively small number of incidents where Serb soldiers were killed and policemen were killed by armed Muslim groups, the response to that seemed to be overwhelming and did result in movements out of population, people move to detention camps and the like. So maybe if that's an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, in your military training, I suspect that you learned what your obligation as a commander of a unit would be, if that unit were attacked in any way, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And not just military training, but practicality, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sometimes those are called standing orders; sometimes I think they're called rules of engagement. Sometimes they're just common sense. But as a practical matter, if you are the commander of a unit that has come under attack, isn't it true that it's your obligation as the commander to completely reduce the threat so that your unit is no longer subject to being attacked? That means disarming, capturing, eliminating the opposing force so that the area is safe and the chances of your coming under attack again are reduced dramatically. Isn't that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, militaries do have standing rules or rules of engagement, as they're often called, which dictate the level of force that can be applied in certain circumstances or certain events. Those rules of engagement from my own experience vary, depending upon the type of conflict, the type of situation. But if I can draw you back to the report and what I'm dealing with here, and if you look, for example, in Prijedor Municipality, which is an example where there were deaths of Serb soldiers by Muslim groups, the Serb documentation itself talks about planned operation, before those actions had occurred, before the soldiers were killed, planned operations to disarm the non-Serb -- or to carry out disarmament operations in Prijedor Municipality in accordance with the ARK Crisis Staff decisions, that those were planned prior to the attack on Hambarine, for example. I believe one or two CSB documents talk the planned operation was due to take place on the 22nd of May, but that the shooting at the Hambarine checkpoint disrupted that plan. So bringing it back to my report, I haven't seen rules of engagement, specific rules of engagement as I would know, from my experience. And, and -- but to answer your question in a hypothetical way, yes, we have rules of engagement, clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, and in that context, if you're attacked, you might very well -- you certainly probably are going to return fire, going to, if possible, capture those people that are assaulting you, and confine them as prisoners, keep them from doing it again, especially if you're dealing with guerrilla kinds of operations -- armed groups that go in and out of the hills, that sort of thing. True? I don't want to dwell on this for a long time?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may be true, but I want to draw it back to the report and the documents that I've seen it. And I leave it to the Court, of course, to make any judgement on the issues of proportionality or otherwise. But what I do see in a number of municipalities like Prijedor and -- or in Kljuc, for example, relatively from a military perspective, relatively low-level action against Serb forces and large-scale military operations over in some cases a protracted period of time, over -- well, initially successful over a couple of days, but then follow-on operations, a large movement out and often of personnel to various detention centres and collection sites, the use of armour or artillery in response to relatively -- relatively low-level incidents which from my military perspective, you know, is not something I would have expected to see from the rules of engagement that I have been used to and the likes. But I clearly leave it to the Court to make the issues of proportionality. But what I do see a number -- not all, about in a number of municipalities, Serb soldiers and Serb policemen were killed, and this large military operation that resulted in large numbers of people being moved out, destruction of property referred to, the movement of people to detention centres --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think you've both made your point. So let's move ahead, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Staying in paragraph 2.76, you say this: "In some municipalities such as Prnjavor or Celinac, for example, there were no such incidents; yet, the areas were subjected to similar military attacks." You don't footnote that. What's your support for there having been similar military attack in Celinac Municipality? Where do you get that idea?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I have -- there is a couple of references to operations in and around the Kotor Varos area, and those instructions talk about operations in Celinac, too. I'd have to go back over there and find out where they are. I'm a little bit unclear myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I suggest to you that there was no military attack in Celinac ever. I put that to you. And again, if you want to go find something that you think supports that statement and give it to Mr. Nicholls --

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will prefer to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- You can certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I know there were military operations in Celinac from the documents I've seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You may be speaking about the Sugic brothers and an attack that they themselves did on a village in the Celinac area. Does that ring a bell with you?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of the Sugic case in terms of the Court records, but I know that there were military operations in Celinac and in particular areas that bordered on the Kotor Varos municipality the borders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [No microphone] In respect to this, perhaps if -- in this case regarding Celinac, and in the previous instance where you referred the witness to carry out further researches and then hand information to Mr. Nicholls, I would prefer if we set a deadline for this. And secondly if they are made available to you, Mr. Nicholls, that you file a note confirming this. And if you do not receive any such information from the witness, that you still file a note confirming that you haven't received such information. Is that agreeable to both of you, Mr. Ackerman, and Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The whole idea is not to leave the matter in doubt, not knowing whether we're still supposed to wait for it, for the information, whether the witness is ready, whether he is not ready. That way, we'll set a dead. And when you've finished giving your testimony, I will ask you to set yourself a deadline and tell us what the deadline should be, how much time you require, in other words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Your Honour. Again, this may be another example where my language is slightly nuanced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, it's important for us to have this cleared up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm just not eager to open up another session of direct or cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, it's a question of -- it's a question I myself don't recall, for example, an attack on Celinac. I'm speaking out of my memory, of course. But I do not exclude that there may have been some documents which the witness may have checked or consulted. And I think that needs to be cleared up. So we'll give the witness enough time to do that, and then you confirm to the Trial Chamber and to the Defence whether the information has been forthcoming or not and what kind of information, if at all. All right? Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 2.91 on page 94, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you think you'll finish today, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've got about four more pages of notes, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Close.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before 2.91, you had been talking about the massacre at Koricanske Stijene on Vlasic mountain. The first thing I think you'll agree with me about is that there is no evidence whatsoever that any army personnel were involved in these killings, is there?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from the documentation I've seen. I haven't seen direct references to army personnel being involved in that killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if you look at 2.91, you say this: "Even though it was possible that no soldiers from the area were involved in this crime and that the local commander probably did enough in reporting the details, it is clear that General-Major Talic did the bare minimum in reacting to this event. Details were passed to the Main Staff but little else was done." When you use this language, even though it was possible that no soldiers from the area were involved, it seems to me you're trying to give the impression -- although it's possible they weren't, it's highly likely that they were, and you have no evidence whatsoever to support the assertion that it's highly likely that they were. It seems like you're trying to leave it ambiguous so that the Trial Chamber might believe that the army was involved in that massacre.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know -- I don't know the full details of the event. I'm going by the documentation. And it was possible that soldiers were not involved in it. But, you know, I'm leaving open to whatever the evidence may say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it would seem to me that if that's what you know, that the sentence you would write was "even though there is no evidence that soldiers from the area were involved," rather than saying "it's possible that they weren't." It raises the probability that they were, and I don't think you have any source for that at all, do you?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all I can say from the event was that a convoy went through a military zone, that Bosko Peulic, the commander in the local area, was aware of the incident, and the documents say that the MUP had been involved. That's all I can really take you to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you looked at any of the testimony in this case about it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't, in fact, looked at the testimony in this case for this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. There's a section where you say this. It's the same sentence. "The local commander probably did enough in reporting the details." Do you think it might have been more fair and accurate to say "the local commander clearly did his duty in reporting the details"? Because the military had no jurisdiction over police activities, nor arrest authority. They could only report what was done. And the local commander did his duty by reporting this.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the relationship between the police and the military is in terms of their responsibility, or the duties, or whether a short report from -- paragraphed report from Colonel Peulic was enough or what other activities he should have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, in --

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: He clearly reported the incident through the chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In 2.90, you refer to a document, a 1st Krajina Corps document. It's in footnote 434. This document reports a massacre in the Skender Vakuf area of over 150 men. This action caused indignation not only among citizens but also among 1st Krajina Corps soldiers. This dark stain which was created did not have support, but it's very fortunate that the international community did not find out about it in more detail. So General Talic is reporting that to the Main Staff, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. I'd have to check the document again, but I think it is a report that goes to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And again, that's his duty, his duty is to report incidents like this to the Main Staff. And you refer to what he did as the bare minimum. But if he had done more, I mean, wasn't it his duty to report it and await orders from the Main Staff as to whether he should do more? I mean, once he reported it, wasn't he in a position to await orders from the Main Staff? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the emphasis in the report is that the reference that it's fortunate that the international community didn't find out about it more detail is somewhat revealing. Also, I believe General Talic later on was interviewed, and the question was put to him, and he made, you know -- he didn't I believe say that, you know, this has been fully investigated and I have done my part or whatever. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The whole point, if the soldiers were not involved, if the army was not involved in the Mount Vlasic massacre, what did you expect more from General Talic than what he actually did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, going by the regulations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because -- which regulations? I mean, he was -- none of his men were responsible for this massacre. Proper reporting of the event seemed to have been done or made. I mean, what else was he supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have said that he appeared to have done the bare minimum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you consider that to be the bare minimum, what goes beyond that which would have been acceptable behaviour to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In terms of his own command, his own instructions, I see very little emphatic reporting following on from this event down his own instructions and his own corps saying this type of behaviour is absolutely intolerable. I have already made the Main Staff informed of this and any type of activity that comes out in a similar manner will be prosecuted through the military chain. Highlighting this sort of activity through his own chain, flagging it up to his soldiers to say this is going on and we are not going to be tarnished with this type of activity. I don't see any of that. What I see is a comment by one of his staff officers in his report that, in essence, saying thank goodness the international community didn't find out about it or we really would have been in trouble. And that's what I mean by the bare minimum. Yes, maybe by regulations and in terms of reporting up the chain, that was it. But it seems to me that this is a particularly -- a particularly notorious incident, particularly important because it was made known to the international community later on. And it seems that what happened was that it was reported up the military chain and forgotten about. And when you place that incident, which is the reason I flagged it up, alongside, for example, Vecici, in Kotor Varos a month or two later which did involve the military and which was a massacre of a similar magnitude, we have reporting General Talic simply articulated that massacre as some kind of combat casualties. So that is my point, I think, in raising this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You've made that clear. We'll have a break --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I ask just one more question and then we'll go to a different subject. I'll just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Ackerman. Except I need the thumbs up from the interpreters for a further question before we -- and the technicians?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just three or four minutes, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, let's proceed, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Still talking about this incident at Koricanske Stijene, did you know, in fact, that army personnel assisted some of the victims who survived that, took statements from them, assisted them getting to medical treatment? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that in a recent -- in a recent transcript by following the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour, for right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just wonder during the break I could speak to Mr. Brown confined only to the additional documentation we have been invited to provide just in case we're able to do it today or immediately. Otherwise, I'm happy to wait. But during the break, I -- we might be able to find --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I would rather, until he finishes his testimony, I would rather if you have any indication that you can give to Mr. Brown, you can make a statement here in open Court. It will achieve the same result --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't have right off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- And I think it's more correct. So let's have a 25-minute break, and then we hope to finish with your testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I bring something to your attention before Mr. Ackerman starts. We have been informed by victim witness that our witness for tomorrow is delayed in Zagreb. There's some sort of problem with the flight. It won't be here until much later this afternoon. We have yet to proof this witness and was wondering if there would be any way, and I bring this up believing that you have a sentencing proceedings tomorrow afternoon wondering if there was a way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not sentencing, I have a Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I know you're looking forward to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: But I was wondering if there was any way we could sit in the afternoon, if those settings could be switched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: During this break, I was discussing with my -- a member of my legal staff, tomorrow's Status Conference, the details, going through the agenda bit by bit. And I don't anticipate that Status Conference to be over in a short time. I reckon I need an hour and a half, two hours for it easily. And that's if everything goes -- runs smoothly. In other words, if no new problems arise and no new submissions are made, and I'm told to expect anything. So I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's try and do this: Let's see if we can switch the Status Conference to the first part of the day, or the morning, 9.00. Then try and start Brdjanin, say, at 11.30. That should give you enough time between this afternoon and tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: We'll do our best, Your Honour. We appreciate you're making the effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if we start at 11.30 with Brdjanin, then we don't need to stay here until 7.00 in the afternoon. We'll have the part of the afternoon session, say we start at 3.00 instead of 2.15. And we go right through 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That sounds very fair to us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I'm just looking to my right at the moment. I haven't consulted --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would think it's not a problem. I can't give a definitive answer right now, but I would think we would be flexible and work with whichever hours work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start from here. Let's start from here. Madam Chuqing, we need to verify. Availability of courtroom should not be a problem because I was sitting in the morning and in the afternoon in any case. So I had the whole courtroom available. With regard to availability of counsel, we only need a confirmation from Mr. Nicholls. Will you be in charge of the cross-examination of the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that's why I hesitate, because it's not my witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If you can check that out for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We're doing that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Assuming we start at 11.30 and continue then at 3.00 until 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This witness is going to last for how many days?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: He's scheduled for two to three days, and we anticipate it will last a day and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So we better not take risks. That's number 2. Then availability of interpreters and technical staff, plus, which is very important, in the Status Conference that I have, it shouldn't make any difference to the accused because he's defending himself. But there is one lawyer that the Trial Chamber has appointed as an amicus curiae, not exactly so, and we must make sure of his availability. And in any case, he needs to be notified. Okay? Otherwise, I think it is feasible. And I also want to make sure that the fact that we'll be sitting until, say, quarter to 2.00 in the morning, in the Brdjanin case, and then resume at 3.00 does not in any way create any difficulties for Mr. Brdjanin to have his lunch and whatever. It's all right if we don't have enough time to have lunch ourselves, but we can't allow that to extend also to the accused. So yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I can give you an answer right now. That's fine with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So provided we have interpretation services plus also the other services. We don't have the same problem.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I don't see any problem there in the interpretation and other services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I need the confirmation. Also, all the technical services that we need for a sitting must be in place, and we must have that assurance. Okay, yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, I just wanted to say thank you to the Chamber for your efforts and working with our schedule. We really appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's continue, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Brown, we're nearing the end of this. I've just got a few more things to talk to you about. We've heard over and over throughout this case about the huge military capabilities of the VRS, tanks, artillery, sometimes perhaps even some air support. And we've also heard about the Muslim forces in the Krajina area, hunting rifles primarily, maybe some old World War II weapons. Those are the kind of things that have been set out for this Trial Chamber. I want to refer you to paragraph 2.92 because this is something that has always baffled me and maybe you can help us with it. You're talking about the village of Vecici: "The local non-Serb population had armed and defended Vecici through the summer months, through the summer months - in other words all summer - they held out there against this vaunted VRS." How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the exact details from the defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I see Mr. Brdjanin waving his arms. I think he's indicating that he can't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No B/C/S translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No B/C/S translation. I'll say something in the hope that the translation now is functioning, is reaching Mr. Brdjanin. Can you hear anything, Mr. Brdjanin? You haven't touched any of those buttons. Is it on the right number? Can we have another set of earphones. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's okay now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's proceed. Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you were starting to answer the question. Just to make sure that it gets translated, you said that "the local non-Serb population had armed and defended Vecici through the summer months, throughout the summer months." And I'd asked you basically how that happened, how they were able to hold out there against the VRS for that long of a time.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I don't actually have that much information from the defenders' perspective, and I can only go on the documents that I've seen, they may well have organised themselves into some defensive structure that held out. I know the area is also particularly mountainous and wooded. And I don't believe there are many roads that really run through there. It may well have been terrain that suited the defender, to be honest. That type of terrain may well have suited those who knew the area well. And hence, the reason they were able to hold out for some time. I do know that some of the VRS documents -- come autumn, we're talking about -- this military -- the 1st Krajina Corps documents themselves, talk about the fact that food was low, and morale was low, and obviously there was a negotiation process going on as can be seen from some of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 2.103, and I hope we can move through this fairly quickly because it's a fairly simple point. You quote from a document, and the document is P661. And I don't need show it to you unless you want to see it. You talk about categorising of prisoners. And the first document you refer to is the Sanski Most Crisis Staff that categorised prisoners into three categories. First category: Politicians; second category, nationalist extremists; and third category, people unwelcome in Sanski Most Municipality, which might include you and me. You then, after speaking of that, go to paragraph 2.105 and say: "This categorisation - the one you referred to there - is similar to that reported in a Banja Luka CSB document reporting on Omarska camp." And then you again quote that, and again, if you want to look at the document, we can make it available to you. But there, there are three categories which maybe is all you're referring to with regard to similarity. But beyond that, I see absolutely nothing similar between those two categorisations, do you?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you say, there are three categories which are for both. And category one in the Omarska camp -- reporting on Omarska camp talks about people who have directly organised and taken part -- or organised, presumably referring to politicians. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's a bit of a stretch, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you may be quibbling over the word "similar." There is a categorisation process going on in two municipalities. These categorisations are broken down into three areas. So if you want to quibble over the word "similar" then yes, maybe you have a point. But I don't think I'm necessarily saying more than just there was a categorisation process that seemed to be going on in two municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talk then in 2.106 about significant cooperation and coordination between the military police and civilian bodies in relation to the establishment of camps. And in 2.108, you talk about military cooperation with the police and civilian bodies with regard to Omarska camp, which you say was established after a Prijedor Crisis Staff decision as a result of Keraterm camp not being able to hold enough prisoners. The document regarding that is P1237. I'd like you to take a look at P1237, please. Now, this document is dated 31 May 1992. And this is not a Prijedor Crisis Staff document, but a Prijedor public security station, SJB, document. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It refers in the first paragraph to a decision of the Crisis Staff, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's what you mean when you say "after a Prijedor Crisis Staff decision in late May...", I think?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You also tell us that it was -- that decision was a result of Keraterm camp not being able to hold enough prisoners. That language isn't in this particular document, is it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I believe it's in another CSB document, talking about the role of the CSB in Prijedor. I'd have to go back to my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you to do that because I'm not particularly interested in that. Now, this document is issued by Simo Drljaca, the chief of the SJB in Prijedor, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm interested in having you look at paragraphs 15 and 16 on page 3 of this document where Drljaca says this: "I most strictly prohibit" -- this is after he has ordered the setting up of this camp at Omarska. "I most strictly prohibit giving any information whatsoever concerning the functioning of this collection centre. All official documents shall be kept at the collection centre and may be taken out or destroyed only with the permission of the chief of the Prijedor public security station - in other words him. This shall be the responsibility of the public security staff." And then in 16, he says this: "I demand most energetically that all the personnel and authorised officials in particular strictly observe these instructions. Failure to do so shall result in severe disciplinary and other measures." And when he says strictly observe these instructions, he's obviously referring to the prohibition of giving any information whatsoever concerning the functioning of this collection centre. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 16 doesn't necessarily indicate that it's exclusively to do with paragraph 15. It may well be that paragraph 16 has to do with the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I totally agree with that. I hope I didn't suggest that it only had to do with 15.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It clearly has to do with the whole document, including 15. Agreed?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it would appear to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We can see then on the last page the distribution list for this. The Crisis Staff received it, the security services coordinators received it, the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka, the police chief, the security chief, and the general manager of the mines. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the distribution list says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It appears that Drljaca was trying to keep knowledge about what was happening here in this Omarska, as he calls it, collection centre, I think, keep what was happening there, the fact of its existence or anything else, pretty much under wraps, prohibiting any information from being given out about it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he clearly states in paragraph 16 that information concerning the functioning of the centre should be -- should be prohibited. But your question -- clearly on the distribution list, it goes to wider than just himself. It's going to a large number of people, Security Services Centre Banja Luka, presumably his superior headquarters. It's going to military personnel from the distribution list. Clearly, the Crisis Staff in Prijedor presumably is getting a copy. And the manager from the iron ore facility and -- where the camp was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay, I'm finished with that document now. I want to go now to Document P380.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would also, just to add, clearly the issue of Omarska camp was not kept exclusively to Simo Drljaca. There are references in military documents about Omarska camp not long after this. And clearly, later on, it became exceptionally well known in terms of press reporting and the like. So it didn't appear to be kept exclusively within his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the press reporting didn't appear until, like, August, I don't think, did it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's true. But the references in the military documents were occurring -- referencing Omarska camp prior to August.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I mean, this secrecy he was trying to enforce might explain why it did take until August for the press or anybody else to find out about that camp. Let me ask you this --

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could have been a contributing factor, but also I do know that the press were exempt from RS territory for a period of time, and the fact that the press couldn't get there at all may have been also a reason why it wasn't reported. But it strays from the parameters of my report to talk about that because I'm not as aware of the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware that the -- that the ICRC had had -- had heard rumours about such a camp in the latter part of July, spent a lot of time looking for it and were unable to find it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You should have now Document P380. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm interested in paragraph 3 of that document, I think. Yes, it's the paragraph that begins with "within the Banja Luka region..." The next sentence: "A portion of the Muslim and Croatian population is moving out, and the region of Bosnian Krajina has issued a decision to facilitate such departures providing that the Serbs from Central Bosnia and places with predominantly Muslim and Croatian populations were also allowed to move out. Those departing will not be allowed to return." You see that?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It seems to be saying "we'll let Muslims and Croats go to Central Bosnia if the authorities in Central Bosnia will let Serbs from there come here," doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's part of what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's the part I'm interested in. And what I'm going to suggest to you is this: We've seen --

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wonder if I could finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd argue it's only just part of the comment. It's putting a restriction saying that process can happen only if Serbs are allowed to leave. So there is a qualification there. And obviously, the last sentence, those departing will not be allowed to return, I think is particularly important, bearing in mind your comments earlier on about refugees and people moving out and war. This for me cuts back as much to some of the discussions that were happening at the 16th Assembly session --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's where I was just going. You beat me there.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Where you had people like Miroslav Vjestica talking about Bosanska Krupa and people not being allowed to return. Resettlement and my issue earlier on that yes, there may well have been significant numbers that did feel they wanted to move out because of the war. But that when you put this type of document and others in context with what was said at the 16th Assembly session on the issue of resettlement, people not being allowed to return, Miroslav's comment about people not coming back, I think it is key to understanding the issues relating to the movement out of the population in the Krajina area and that this was as much about moving those people out and ensuring a Serb state that they controlled. As Karadzic saying, they don't want large number of people who are in a state who are against that state. So I think this statement, yes, there is an element of people moving from Serb areas into non-Serb areas, but there is also this issue that these people are not going to be returning. And I think that is as important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you were thinking of a different part of the 16th Assembly session than I was, but let me suggest this to you. You'll recall that General Mladic at that session said: Better -- I'm just going to paraphrase it now, but. Better to have them with us than over there in the trenches fighting against us. And I suggest to you that what's being said here is what dictated a great deal of what was going on; that was a fear that if Serbs were allowed to leave the Muslims areas of Bosnia, they would wind up in a VRS, a fear that if Muslims and Croats were allowed to leave the Bosnian Krajina, they would wind up in the Croatian and Bosnian armies. And that would explain why men of military age were held in places like Manjaca, regardless of whether they had been combatants or not in some cases, I think. That would explain this statement in here, saying, okay, we'll send some people over there who might be soldiers for you, but you got to send the people who will be soldiers for us back over there. And I think that explains a lot of what was going on over this period of time with regard to these movements of people back and forth between Muslim-controlled areas and Serb-controlled areas, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would agree that from Mladic's statements that he clearly has concerns in those areas, but I would disagree that that was the primary reason. I think that through the documentation I have reviewed in the military documents and looking at the 16th Assembly session amongst others, that it's clear that there was a policy to establish control in territory designated as Serb, and that there was a belief and an implementation that a method of control was to move significant numbers of people out of that territory that weren't Serb. And the documents, the military documents themselves talk about mass departures, emigration, organised removal, those not being allowed to return, destruction of property, the involvement of the military police, and as noted here, civilian instruction, about the facilitation to remove people who they believed -- that they wanted to remove from territory that was to be controlled by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I assume you'd also concede that there are a number of documents that deal with the difficulty people had who were trying to leave -- being able to leave. They were not permitted to leave. I'm talking about Muslims from the Krajina were not permitted to leave. Do you recall any of those documents?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any specifically. If you have some to show me, then I'm more than willing to comment on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't want to do that right now. I want to finish with you because I want to make sure we finish today if we can. I want to go to 2.161 for the final thing that I want to ask you about. Beginning at 2.161, you speak about a visit by Cyrus Vance and David Owen to Banja Luka on 25 September 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And during that meeting, they met with a number of people. Among them, the Mufti Halilovic, the bishop of Banja Luka, Catholic bishop of Banja Luka, and so forth, right?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Plus the orthodox bishop. And at page 122, you quote from Lord Owen's book the following: "We had one meeting which gave us a measure of hope with the Roman Catholic Bishop, the Muslim Mufti, and the orthodox bishop of Banja Luka, all three of whom were unanimous in saying that totally unacceptable pressure was being put on both Muslims and Croats in villages around Banja Luka, particularly Prijedor." Now, when he says all three of them, one of those was the orthodox bishop of Banja Luka. Right?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what he says in his book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. And then he goes on to say this: "On whether ethnic cleansing was being applied in Banja Luka itself, there was less unanimity but none of the three denied that undue pressure was present. And then he says he made our intense displeasure abundantly clear to Karadzic. Right?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that's what he writes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So, this indicates there was a great deal of concern of what was going on in places like Prijedor, but less unanimity regarding what was going on in Banja Luka itself?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Less unanimity in relation to ethnic cleansing. That's what he writes in his book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers to my questions. I have no more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Is there re-examination, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour. I won't be able to finish in 10 minutes. I think I probably have -- it's hard to guess because I just have been writing notes. 30 minutes, something like that, or 40. I'm happy to start, but I won't finish in 10 minutes. What I'd like to do is flag up some of the documents which I think the witness referred to but didn't have at his fingertips when he was answering questions, and also there are several areas which I think can be made clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start anyway. We've got 10 minutes, and we'll make use of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was wondering if Mr. Nicholls might give us some idea how long he thinks he will take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 30 to 40 minutes is my guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I missed that, I'm sorry. I can see it now right here in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, the first thing I'd like to do is try to clear up a couple points from yesterday. And the first one relates to paragraph 1.17 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'd like the witness to be shown P365.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were questioned about this area on the transcript page 21491 yesterday. And the assertion by Mr. Ackerman essentially, showing you his Exhibit DB195 which I don't think I need to show you again right now, was that you had insufficiently demonstrated or that your citation did not support adequately that what you say in that paragraph is true, that the 5th Corps, to quote you, and the JNA was adamant, to paraphrase actually, that it would not be withdrawn from Bosnia-Herzegovina at any price. Do you remember that conversation?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, P365 is a document which is footnoted as footnote 21 directly on the next page under paragraph 1.18. Here, both these paragraphs, we're dealing broadly with the 5th Corps development from January to April 1992. If you could just look at P365, which is a 5th Corps command report from the 3rd of April 1992, that's about a week after the date of the report in DB195, 26 of March, does this document also support your conclusion that the 5th Corps was adamant that it was not going to abandon Bosnia-Herzegovina? If I can say, it doesn't speak specifically about leaving, but about a guarantee to the people of the Bosnian Krajina that it will protect them from destruction.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's one of the documents, one of the number of documents that I have seen that talk about this during this period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can we conclude that in paragraph 3 where General Talic who signs this -- writes: "Make sure that the Banja Luka Krajina Corps remain a reliable defender of all peoples and nationalities in the Bosnian Krajina. " They were also talking about the 5th Corps not leaving the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think he's talking about, in essence, maintaining Bosnia with the other republics in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next paragraph that you were questioned about that I want to come back to is paragraph 1.105 in your report. Page 45. And here you were shown the Dzeric instruction footnoted in footnote 151, which is Exhibit Number P157. Mr. Ackerman showed you a document to try to show that this instruction was carried out or followed in Prijedor and to suggest that there was a separation between military and civilian, in terms of chain of command. I'd like to show you P1243. We can put my copy on. It will be quicker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The B/C/S is on the back, so maybe you can flip if he needs to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, can you just - it's a short document - review that for me, give me your assessment about what that document tells us about the separation of the military police and civilian command structures, whether the Prijedor Crisis Staff was able to issue orders to those bodies.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on face value of this document, in June 1992, Milomir Stakic under a decision of the Prijedor Municipality Crisis Staff is issuing an order which is directed to military police and civilian police bodies. And it's distributed to the military command and to the police, and one for the files. So in this case, it would indicate that Prijedor Crisis Staff is giving an instruction of a military -- or to military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I'm correct, you've discussed this topic, not this specific document, but this topic in your testimony in the Stakic case. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe that is at pages 8782 to 89 of that transcript. Finally, well -- you don't need to look at it now, but you were also shown today by Mr. Ackerman P637. Do you remember that document? It's the Sanski Most Crisis Staff decision issuing orders to Colonel Basara of the 6th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I recognise what's happening. I think, though, these questions are kind of silly because I have conceded that these bodies issued orders. My point was they had no effect, nobody followed them. So that's the point I'm trying to make. And I think this is kind of a silly inquiry to go into saying-- cause I've already conceded that can happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Ackerman's point and I suggest he's right. So I suggest you direct, or redirect your questions to cover the last point that Mr. Ackerman points out, namely that they were sort of orders which were in themselves ineffective.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you don't have much time, Mr. Brown, but I'll ask you just regarding the two documents we've talked about. Can you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we're going to stop on schedule, I don't think he can answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's stop here. And we will resume tomorrow at 11.30, as agreed. I'm afraid you will have to come again tomorrow. I had hoped that we would have finished with your testimony today. Unfortunately, that is not the case. In the meantime, should the need arise, just think about how much time you require to conduct further researches on the two matters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.
